answer:
VIABILITY: The revenue mechanics are conceptually clear (hardware kit at ~$450, then ~$120/yr subscription, plus $99 single gloves) and the hardware-plus-recurring-software structure is a sound pattern. But the path to profitable revenue is unproven. Unit economics are thin and mostly unknown: the $38 BOM is a hand-built, wired prototype figure, with no manufacturing quotes. A shippable product needs wireless radios, batteries, charging, durability for contact-sport use, washability, multiple sizes, left/right hands, certification, packaging, and returns/warranty, all of which will raise cost materially. A 6-glove kit at ~$450 implies ~$75/glove retail; after COGS, fulfillment, support, payment fees and channel costs, margin could be slim or negative at low volume. Subscription revenue of ~$120/team/year is small, and the key assumption, that volunteer-run rec programs with tight budgets will renew a software fee, is untested. Churn risk is high because rosters turn over yearly and coach volunteers rotate. Buyers are also fragmented: rec leagues are volunteer-run with small budgets and slow, seasonal purchasing; the person with the pain (coach) is often not the person with the budget (league/parents). Parents buying a $99 glove is plausible but a different, consumer-marketing business.

ASSUMPTION VALIDITY: (1) Demand: 14 coach conversations, mostly local and from the team's network, with 'several' saying they would pay, is stated interest, not purchase intent; no pre-orders, LOIs, pilots with money changing hands. (2) Market sizing: the 'over $1B TAM' is player count x assumed price and the team itself admits it is inflated; the 20-30K program SAM is more credible but unsourced, and with ~$450 kit + ~$120/yr it implies a real SAM of roughly $10-15M in kits and ~$3M/yr recurring, a decent niche but not a venture-scale market unless it expands to other positions/sports. (3) Core value claim: the 0-100 score rests on rules from two coaches, with no validation that glove pressure/motion data actually correlates with good catching technique or improves outcomes. If the score isn't trusted or doesn't produce measurable improvement, the product is a gimmick. This is the single biggest technical/product risk. (4) Financials: $18K year-one revenue from pilots and >$300K by year three are acknowledged as unvalidated; the break-even-by-year-two claim is not supported by any cost build (tooling, inventory, certification, patent, support, salaries). 20 gloves for 4-5 pilot teams would not even cover 6-glove kits for 5 teams, so the pilot plan is tight. (5) Competitive claims: 'not aware of' a competitor is a weak basis; sensor gloves and low-cost computer-vision apps (phone video + AI) could deliver similar coaching without hardware, a real substitution threat at near-zero cost. No patent and no defensible moat beyond execution.

SCALABILITY: Hardware introduces inventory, working-capital, and manufacturing risk that a student team lacks experience to manage, and the team has no manufacturing expertise or advisor. Growth via state-by-state league relationships is plausible but slow, seasonal (one fall buying window), and sales-heavy relative to a $450 ticket, so CAC could exceed first-year margin unless distribution runs through leagues or associations. Software scales well, but the subscription is too small to carry the business; scalability depends on expanding to other positions (QB, DB, linemen), sports, and league-wide licensing, none of which is developed. The data-insights revenue idea is premature and raises privacy concerns because the users are minors.

STRENGTHS: clear, relatable problem; low-cost positioning versus enterprise tools; sensible razor/recurring model; honest self-assessment of gaps (patent, manufacturing, small samples); lean spending and a working prototype; relevant team skills in hardware, software and domain experience.

BOTTOM LINE: Plausible but early and unproven. There is a believable niche and a reasonable model shape, but key assumptions (willingness to pay, score validity, true unit cost, renewal rates, CAC) are untested, and the achievable market is modest. Highest-priority validation steps: get paid pilots or pre-orders, validate the score against expert coach ratings and measured improvement, obtain real manufacturing quotes for a wireless production design, and test league-level purchasing to reduce acquisition cost. Viability is moderate-to-low as currently evidenced; scalability is limited unless the platform broadens beyond a single skill.
